q: Why do employers withhold income tax from each paycheck?
r: To collect tax gradually throughout the year instead of in one lump sum
Withholding spreads the tax payment across the year.
w: To keep the money as a bonus for the company itself
The money goes to the government, not the employer.
To lower the employee's total yearly income by law
Withholding does not change gross income.
To pay the employee in advance for future work
It is a tax payment, not an advance.

q: A worker gets a large refund every spring. What does this suggest about withholding?
r: Too much tax was withheld from paychecks during the year
The refund returns the extra amount withheld.
w: Too little tax was withheld from paychecks all year
That would lead to owing money, not a refund.
The worker did not earn any income last year
A refund comes from overpaid tax.
The employer paid the worker a surprise bonus
A refund is not a bonus.

q: What is self-employment tax?
r: The Social Security and Medicare tax paid by people who work for themselves
Self-employed workers pay both the employee and employer share.
w: A sales tax on products sold at a store
A property tax on a home office
A tax on gifts given to employees

q: What is the main purpose of a resume?
r: To summarize your skills, education and experience for employers
Employers use it to decide who to interview.
w: To list the prices of your services for clients
To report your income to the tax agency
To apply for a bank loan

q: Two job offers pay $38,000. Job A includes health insurance worth $5,000 a year and Job B includes none. Which offer has the higher total value?
r: Job A, because benefits add to total compensation
Benefits are part of what the employer pays.
w: Job B, because it pays the same salary with fewer rules
The salaries are equal, but A adds benefits.
They are exactly equal in value
Neither, because benefits have no value

q: What is job satisfaction mostly influenced by besides pay?
r: Work environment, growth opportunities and how well the job fits your interests
Money is only part of why people enjoy work.
w: The color of the office walls and nothing else
That is too narrow to be the main factor.
The number of coworkers who share a birthday
The length of the commute alone
Commute matters, but many factors count.

q: Why is it smart to keep receipts for major purchases?
r: They prove what you paid and help with returns, warranties and taxes
Receipts serve as proof of purchase.
w: They let you spend the money a second time
A receipt does not refund money.
They are required to be framed by law
They lower the price of the item later

q: What is a store credit card most likely to offer?
r: A discount on purchases at that store, often with a high interest rate
They reward shopping at one retailer but can be costly.
w: Lower interest rates than any bank card always
Store cards often have higher rates.
Free money that never has to be repaid

q: A store offers 'buy now, pay later' with no interest if you pay within 6 months. What risk should a shopper check?
r: Whether deferred interest or fees apply if the balance is not paid in time
Missing the deadline can bring large charges.
w: Whether the store logo is attractive
Whether the shopper has friends who also use it
Friends do not set the terms.
Whether the item is available in other colors
Colors do not affect the financing risk.

q: What does it mean to live within your means?
r: Spending no more than you earn
It keeps you out of unmanageable debt.
w: Spending more than you earn to feel successful

q: Which is the best example of delayed gratification in spending?
r: Saving for several months to buy a quality item instead of buying a cheaper one now
Waiting can lead to a better choice.
w: Buying the first item you see on a whim
Spending your whole paycheck the day you get it
Charging a purchase to a card you cannot repay

q: A teen can spend $100 on concert tickets or save it toward a $400 laptop needed for school. What is the opportunity cost of buying the tickets?
r: Progress toward the laptop that the $100 would have funded
The best alternative use of the money is given up.
w: Nothing, because tickets are a want and not a need
Every choice has an opportunity cost.
The price of the laptop plus tax
That is the cost of the laptop, not of the choice.
The cost of parking at the concert

q: Why is a savings account safer than keeping large amounts of cash at home?
r: Deposits are protected by FDIC insurance and cannot be lost in a theft or fire
Insured accounts protect up to the limit.
w: Cash at home earns higher interest than an account
Banks never charge any fees on savings
Savings accounts cannot be used for emergencies
They can be used for emergencies.

q: Which statement about interest on savings is correct?
r: Interest is money the bank pays you for keeping funds on deposit
It is a reward for letting the bank use your money.
w: Interest is a fee you pay for opening an account
That would be an account fee.
Interest is a tax you owe on your balance each month
Interest is the amount you deposit every month

q: Priya deposits $2,000 at 3% compounded annually. About how much will she have after 2 years?
r: About $2,122
$2,000 grows to $2,060, then to about $2,122.
w: That is after only one year.
That uses a much higher rate.

q: What is a good way to avoid dipping into savings for small wants?
r: Keep a separate account for goals and a small budget for fun spending
Separate funds make limits clear.
w: Keep all money in one account and never track it
Carry large amounts of cash everywhere

q: What does FDIC insurance cover?
r: Deposits in insured banks up to the legal limit if the bank fails
It protects depositors, not investments.
w: Stocks bought through a bank's brokerage
Investments are not insured by the FDIC.
Losses caused by a drop in the market
Cash kept in a safe at home

q: Why can closing an old credit card account sometimes lower a credit score?
r: It can shorten credit history and raise credit utilization
Both factors influence scores.
w: Closed accounts are always deleted from reports at once
Banks punish customers for canceling cards
Scores are calculated by formula, not punishment.
Old accounts are not counted in any score

q: A person with a 620 credit score and one with a 780 score both apply for a $15,000 car loan. Which is more likely to get a lower interest rate?
r: The person with the 780 score, because lenders see less risk
Higher scores usually earn better rates.
w: The person with the 620 score, because lenders need customers
Both will receive exactly the same rate
Both may qualify, at different rates.

q: What is a variable interest rate?
r: A rate that can go up or down over time based on market conditions
Payments can change.
w: A rate that never changes during the loan
A rate that is always zero
A rate chosen by the borrower

q: What is a fixed interest rate?
r: A rate that stays the same for the full loan term
Payments are predictable.
w: A rate that changes each month with the market
A rate that is repaid at the end of the loan only
A rate that is free of charge

q: Before taking out a loan, which comparison tells you the true yearly cost of borrowing from different lenders?
r: The annual percentage rate (APR)
APR includes interest and certain fees.
w: The size of the lender's building
This has nothing to do with cost.
The number of branches the lender has
This has nothing to do with cost.
The color of the loan paperwork
This has nothing to do with cost.

q: Why should you review your insurance coverage after a major life change like buying a house?
r: Your needs and the value you need to protect may have changed
Coverage should match your situation.
w: Insurance policies automatically update themselves for free
Policies must be updated by the owner.
Insurance is only needed once in a lifetime

q: A driver causes an accident that injures another person and has only the state minimum liability coverage. What is the main risk?
r: Costs above the policy limits may have to be paid out of pocket
Limits cap what the insurer pays.
w: The insurer will pay unlimited amounts no matter what
The other driver must pay for everything
No costs will be owed because it was an accident

q: Which action reduces the risk of a home fire?
r: Installing working smoke detectors and not overloading outlets
Prevention lowers risk.
w: Storing flammable liquids near a heater
Removing the batteries from smoke detectors
Leaving candles burning when you sleep

q: What is self-insurance?
r: Setting aside your own money to cover possible losses
Emergency savings can serve this role.
w: Buying a policy from an insurance company
Asking a friend to promise to pay

q: Which loss is best handled by buying insurance rather than saving for it?
r: A rare event that could cost far more than you could ever save
Insurance protects against catastrophic loss.
w: A small cost you can easily pay from savings
A regular expense that happens every month
A cost you choose to avoid completely

q: What does it mean when an investment is liquid?
r: It can be sold quickly for cash without a big loss in value
Stocks on major exchanges are fairly liquid.
w: It is stored as water or fluid
This is not the financial meaning.
It cannot be sold for years

q: Which is usually the most liquid asset?
r: Cash in a checking account
It is available immediately.
w: It may take time to sell.

q: An investor puts all their money into one company's stock and the company fails. Which investing principle did they ignore?
r: Diversification
Spreading money reduces the harm from one failure.

q: What is a stock market index?
r: A measure of the performance of a group of stocks
The S&P 500 is an example.

q: What is rebalancing a portfolio?
r: Adjusting investments back to your target mix of assets
It controls risk drift over time.
w: Selling everything and starting over each year

q: A long-term investor sees the market drop 15% in a month. Which response is generally most sensible?
r: Stay with the plan and keep investing regularly if the goals have not changed
Reacting emotionally can lock in losses.
w: Sell everything immediately out of fear
Borrow money to buy a single stock
Stop looking at the plan and give up on the goal

q: What does the saying 'don't put all your eggs in one basket' mean for investing?
r: Spread your money across different investments
Diversification lowers risk.
w: Buy only one stock you trust
Spend all your money on eggs

q: What is the main benefit of an employer 401(k) match?
r: It adds extra money to your retirement savings for free
Not contributing enough can leave match money unclaimed.
w: It lowers your income tax to zero
It lets you withdraw anytime without rules

q: Two investors each save $200 a month for 30 years. One earns 4% and the other 7%. Which result is most likely?
r: The 7% investor ends with a much larger balance because of compounding
Higher returns compound into big differences.
w: Both end with the same balance
The 4% investor ends with a larger balance

q: What is a bear market?
r: A period when stock prices fall significantly, often 20% or more
Investor pessimism is high.
w: A period when prices rise steadily
A period when markets are closed
That is not a bear market.
That is not a financial term.

q: What is a bull market?
r: A period when stock prices are rising or expected to rise
Investor confidence is high.
w: A period when prices fall sharply
A period when prices never change
That is not a financial term.

q: What is a stock split?
r: A company increases the number of shares and lowers each share's price proportionally
Total value stays the same.
w: A company gives away half its profits
A company merges with a rival

q: Which statement about past investment performance is accurate?
r: It does not guarantee future results
Markets change.
w: It guarantees the same results next year
It is the only factor that matters
It proves an investment cannot lose money

q: Which choice best protects the buying power of long-term savings from inflation?
r: Investing in a diversified mix that has historically outpaced inflation
Cash alone tends to lose purchasing power.
w: Keeping all savings in cash for decades
It loses value and is unsafe.

q: What is a good first step to take control of your spending?
r: Track what you spend for a month to see where your money goes
Awareness comes before change.

q: What is the best way to avoid paying credit card interest?
r: Pay the full statement balance by the due date every month
This avoids interest on purchases.
w: Pay only the minimum each month
Late payments add fees and interest.
Use the card only for cash advances

q: What is a cash advance on a credit card?
r: Borrowing cash against your credit limit, usually with fees and immediate interest
It is one of the most expensive ways to borrow.
w: Paying a bill early with your own money

q: What is the difference between earned income and unearned income?
r: Earned income comes from working; unearned income comes from sources like interest or dividends
Both can be taxable.
w: Earned income is never taxed; unearned is always taxed
Earned income comes from gifts; unearned from jobs

q: What is the purpose of an emergency fund in relation to spending?
r: It helps cover unplanned costs so you do not need to use credit
It protects your budget.
w: It is meant for planned vacations
It is meant to grow quickly through risky bets
It replaces the need for insurance
